PART TWO: Some suggestions on preparing to treat this at home.

This is from my personal experience. I want to hear feedback, especially from medical professionals. I help multiple relatives with oxygen on a daily basis, but I have never weathered a pandemic or dealt with COVID-19.

Some cases can be treated at home if the have the right training and equipment. Obviously some cases will be mild and some will be severe. There will be many cases so mild this training and equipment would not be used, and other cases so severe that this training and equipment would be insufficient. There are cases where this equipment would let the patient at home instead of needing medical help. Every patient we successfully treat at home is a victory in the fight against COVID-19.

Everyone in your household should be preparing to treat pneumonia at home. People need to know how to do the following without infecting themselves:

* take vitals,

* give oxygen if the equipment is available,

* prepare meals, and

* make sure sick people keep hydrated,

* disinfect surfaces,

* do laundry,

* wash dishes,

* clean up messes caused by sick people, and

* know when to call emergency services.

* They should have everyone's medical history ready in neatly printed formats including their doctors, conditions, medications, and recent vitals.

Because children and teens usually get less severe cases, they may be the only ones standing in some households. (I am referring to households where one or more sickly or elderly people care for children.) The children should be trained as far as they can. If you are concerned about traumatizing them, I promise that seeing grandma die will traumatize them more then learning to care for grandma when she is sick.

In a perfect world, every household would have an oxygen concentrator. These machines use electricity to push air through a special membrane that only allows the oxygen (O2) through. This stream of oxygen is fed to the patient, usually with a nasal canula. Many people will still have these from deceased relatives, or will have one that a sick relative does not use. Low blood oxygen content (hypoxia) is how pneumonia kills people and damages their organs. Keeping the patient's oxygen up is a critical part of treatment.

  • Using an oxygen concentrator if the patient's oxygen saturation is above 90% is not helpful; they do not need it.
  • If a patient's O2 level is below 90%, and an oxygen concentrator can bring it above 90%, get them an oxygen concentrator. Adjust the O2 level (liters per minute) until their O2 level is above 90%.
  • If the patient's O2 is still below 90%, call their doctor.
  • If the patient's O2 is below 70%, call emergency services.
  • If the patient's O2 is below 50%, brain damage will occur.
  • A recent drop in O2 levels can signal a coming sharp drop, so closely monitor anyone whose O2 level has dropped in the last several hours. Do not go to bed and leave them!

Generally, oxygen concentrators that roll across the floor and are about 30" tall can put out 6 liters per minute of 100% O2. The large ones are usually rated for continuous use, so you can plug them in and run them. They are available on CraigsList used for $200 or less. These are generalizations; every model of oxygen concentrator is different.

Small (10 pound or less) oxygen concentrators the size of a 6-pack cooler generally put out 3 liters per minute or less at 30% O2 or less. Most of the small portable machines are not rated to run continuously. They may stall due to thermal issues within an hour. Portable machines are still available on Amazon, for a few hundred dllars. These are generalizations; every model of oxygen concentrator is different.

I would much prefer a larger, floor-standing model over a similarly priced portable model.

Oxygen bottles are available, but even a large E bottle with a conserving regulator will only last 8 hours. They are a decent back-up, and can help when the power is out. They could also, hypothetically, be used to help a second sick person in the household.

Both kinds need tubing to take the oxygen from the machine to a canula that feeds the oxygen up the patient's nose. This is uncomfortable for the first few minutes or hours, but patients get used to it. The oxygen goes up the patient's nose, and helps their (in the case of pneumonia) diseased lungs get more oxygen into their blood stream.

Make sure you have sufficient tubing and canulas. Canulas are usually replaced weekly or less often than that. Different canulas are preferred by different patients. This is a subjective issue of patient comfort.

There are full face masks used to deliver oxygen. I am not a fan of them. This is a subjective issue of patient comfort.

Oxygen is very dry and can dry out nasal passages and cause nosebleeds. Most floor standing oxygen concentrators have optional bottles to bubble the oxygen though water to reduce this problem. This is a subjective issue of patient comfort.

Keep oxygen away from flames. Bottles of oxygen can greatly increase the O2 levels in a room or building and lead to severe fires. Oxygen concentrators send O2 down the tube that was pulled from the air, so a few feet from the patient the O2 levels are normal with no increase risk of fire. Of course the tubing blowing oxygen can still cause problems with open flames.

Oxygen concentrators are prescription only in some areas, and are freely available in other areas. They are generally available online in all areas regardless of legal technicalities.
